notes: Original fictional café route; the schematic is a spatial teaching diagram, not an asserted map of actual Recife or a coastline. No audio, paid images, adaptation, authentic quotation or brevity/exercise waiver.
Two distinct paper maps are made; Ana carries hers, Bia retains hers. Bia carries Rosa’s phone with her knowledge, and Rosa retains the two café keys. The courtyard gate is only seen from outside.
Actual ao/à directional uses, not old article-a tokens, provide the new preposition’s teaching. Clear English senses support ambiguous noun banks under current RULES.md.

The generic checker folds à to a, so its a-preposition token total includes old article-a occurrences. Actual ao/à movement clauses, the direction frames and construction drills establish the new meaning independently. Seven notes supplement the delivered route/action diagrams despite the advisory low gloss ratio.

Post-review: vir is speaker-centred or tied to a clearly established narrative viewpoint; the listener’s location alone is not its rule. Complete-answer prefix hints are removed; construction cues remain, and Pensum A has separate worked models for contractions and verb transformations.

review_questions.question: RQ-1: Check actual ir/vir/seguir forms, deictic viewpoints, G07 a/para and a+article ao/à (including right/left frames), all English teaching claims and translations.

RQ-2: Check first-use inference for all route/landmark nouns and movement; verify the fictional schematic matches both squares, crossings and the return orientation. No real geography claim is intended.

RQ-3: Check paper/map/phone/key custody, evidence by which Bia locates Ana, gate-closed hook without unallocated portão/trancado, all30 scheduled recalls and every exercise key/bank/form; assess substantive reading.

grammar.title: Frase
grammar.rule: Eu vou ao pátio. Você vai à praça. Nós vamos para a ponte.
grammar.note_en:
Ir and vir describe movement from a viewpoint. Eu vou ao pátio means “I go to the courtyard”; nós vamos ao pátio means “we go to the courtyard.” The actual ir forms here are vou with eu, vai with one named person or você, vamos with nós and vão with elas/eles/vocês. Bia vai à ponte means “Bia goes to the bridge”; Elas vão à praça means “They go to the square.” The verb is irregular: do not build these forms from the earlier -ar/-er/-ir endings. The little word ir is the dictionary label for the action, not a new future-tense construction. All the narration remains present.

In these scenes, vir presents an approach toward the speaker, or toward a clearly established character viewpoint in narration. A destination at the listener’s location does not by itself require vir. For example, Você vem para a praça? means “Are you coming to the square?” Ana asks while she is there. Eu vou à ponte means “I go to the bridge,” from Bia’s departure viewpoint. Later Ana vê Bia perto da ponte (“Ana sees Bia near the bridge”) sets Ana’s viewpoint before Bia vem à praça (“Bia comes to the square”). Bia’s question Você vem para a ponte, Ana? (“Are you coming to the bridge, Ana?”) invites Ana to join Bia toward the bridge, with Bia as the reference point. The revised narration explicitly places Bia near the bridge before Ana approaches. The neighbor’s Eu venho ao pátio com Paulo means “I come to the courtyard with Paulo,” describing his usual visits, not claiming Paulo has left the café in this scene. Only the encountered vem/venho cells are introduced here; this is not a whole vir paradigm.

Direction a combines with a following definite article: a + o becomes ao, a + a becomes à. The written grave accent in à marks this combination. Compare Bia está na praça (“Bia is in the square”), with Bia vai à praça (“Bia goes to the square”). Location em + a gives na; movement a + a gives à. Ao mercado means “to the market,” à esquina “to the corner,” ao pátio “to the courtyard,” à rua “to the street,” à ponte “to the bridge.” The noun’s grammatical gender controls the article: praça, rua, ponte and esquina are feminine; mercado, rio, caminho and pátio masculine. Mapa is masculine despite its final a: um mapa, dois mapas (“a map, two maps”). No new object-pronoun a is taught by these directional phrases.

Para can also name the destination: vou para a praça means “I go to the square,” and vamos para a ponte “we go to the bridge.” Para a remains two words in this edited Brazilian register; it does not contract to à. Both a and para can describe a brief trip here. Do not learn an absolute rule that one must mean a short visit and the other a permanent move. The grammatical difference tested in a + a → à is the requested construction, not a claim that para a would make an impossible journey. Para with a noun can also mean “for”: espaço para os livros means “space for the books.” No para plus infinitive purpose clause is introduced.

À direita and à esquerda mean “on/to the right” and “on/to the left,” using a + a before the feminine nouns direita/esquerda. On the schematic, the café is below the market: travelers face toward the market on their first approach. The correct square/courtyard is to the right of the market ON THE PAPER, the bridge and mistaken square to its left. On the return from the bridge, they follow the courtyard path shown on that map; the narrative does not ask them to repeat the same bodily turn while facing a different direction. No real Recife street layout is claimed.

Seguir means following a route or person: Ana segue o caminho means “Ana follows the way”; nós seguimos o mapa means “we follow the map”; vocês seguem Bia means “you follow Bia”; eu sigo você means “I follow you.” Sigo is the actual first-person form, not an unintroduced guess at a regular pattern. Atravessar means crossing: A ponte atravessa o rio means “The bridge crosses/spans the river”; as pessoas atravessam o rio na ponte means “the people cross the river on the bridge.” The same diagram establishes the route over the water. A square’s name alone does not establish its location: two distinct squares have tables, but only one is near the market. Dois mapas names two physical sheets; Ana’s map does not mysteriously remain at the café when she carries it away.

Eu estou means “I am [located/in a state]” and eu vejo “I see”: they are licensed earlier irregular cells actually encountered here, not regular -ar patterns. In Ana’s phone message, Eu estou na praça means “I am in the square”; Eu vejo o rio means “I see the river.” The gate remains closed at arrival. The photo of the courtyard is not evidence that the travelers have entered it; the visible locked gate and waiting preserve the next chapter’s problem.

For the table’s remaining cells, vou/vai/vamos/vão mean “I go / you or he or she goes / we go / they or plural you go”; venho/vem mean “I come / you or he or she comes”; sigo/segue/seguimos/seguem mean “I follow / you or he or she follows / we follow / they or plural you follow.” Para a praça means “to the square,” para a ponte “to the bridge.” The one-person table columns use named people or você, whereas the eu column is the speaker.
